title: Linear algebra as a language for model behavior
summary: Read vectors, matrix products, transposes, and norms as concrete operations on representations.

sections.title: A matrix transforms coordinates
paragraphs: A feature vector is an ordered collection of measurements. Its entries might describe temperature, pressure, and humidity, or learned coordinates with no individual name. A matrix maps one such coordinate system into another. Each output coordinate is a weighted combination of input coordinates. This perspective makes a neural network layer easier to inspect: its weight matrix describes which input directions influence each output, while its bias shifts the result.

sections.title: Follow one multiplication by hand
paragraphs: Let a row vector \(x=[2,-1]\) and a weight matrix \(W=\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\4&2\end{bmatrix}\). Multiplication gives \(xW=[-2,4]\): the first output is \(2\cdot1-1\cdot4\), and the second is \(2\cdot3-1\cdot2\). The transpose swaps rows and columns; it does not invert a transformation. In reverse-mode differentiation, transposes appear because a gradient must travel from output coordinates back into input coordinates.

sections.title: Measure size without losing meaning
paragraphs: The Euclidean norm measures vector length. The Frobenius norm treats a matrix as one long vector, whereas its spectral norm measures the largest possible amplification of a unit input. Those quantities answer different questions: total weight magnitude and worst-direction amplification need not move together. Multiplication is also order-sensitive; changing \(XW\) into \(WX\) can change both meaning and validity. Write the input and output spaces beside every matrix before manipulating an expression.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Use the Linear Algebra chapter of Deep Learning as a notation reference: identify the input and output spaces whenever a matrix appears. Then revisit the example here with basis inputs \([1, 0]\) and \([0, 1]\). They select the two rows of \(W\), so \([2,-1]\) produces twice the first row minus the second. This gives a geometric interpretation of the multiplication and a quick way to detect a mistaken transpose.

For the discussion of norms, construct a comparison that separates total size from maximum amplification: \(\operatorname{diag}(4,0)\) and \(\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt8,\sqrt8)\) both have Frobenius norm 4, but their spectral norms differ. The first map concentrates its strength in one direction; the second spreads it evenly. A weight-size report therefore needs the norm name and a reason for choosing it. None of these matrix measurements, by itself, determines prediction quality after nonlinear layers.

exercise.prompt: For \(W=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&4\end{bmatrix}\), compute its Frobenius and spectral norms. Which unit vector receives the largest amplification?
exercise.answer: The Frobenius norm is \(\sqrt{9+16}=5\). The spectral norm is 4. The unit vector \([0, 1]\) is stretched to \([0, 4]\), achieving that maximum; its negative works as well.

takeaways: Matrix multiplication composes linear maps.
Transpose, inverse, and norm are different operations.

title: Derive tensor shapes before running the model
summary: Use dimensions as a lightweight proof that a computation connects the intended axes.

sections.title: Shapes carry semantic labels
paragraphs: A tensor shape becomes useful when each axis has a name. For a batch of sentences, \([B, T, D]\) means examples, token positions, and features. The identical numerical shape could describe entirely different data, so checking only sizes is insufficient. Shape reasoning follows which axes survive, which are contracted, and which are newly introduced. This often catches an incorrect implementation before any loss curve can reveal it.

sections.title: Trace a projection and a comparison
paragraphs: Suppose \(X\) has shape \([2, 5, 12]\) and \(W\) has shape \([12, 8]\). The product \(XW\) has shape \([2, 5, 8]\); the feature axis contracts while batch and token axes remain. A bias \([8]\) broadcasts over both leading axes. To compare every token with every other token, multiply \(Q\) of shape \([2, 5, 8]\) by \(K\) transposed on its final two axes, obtaining scores \([2, 5, 5]\).

sections.title: Broadcasting can hide an error
paragraphs: Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right. Two axes are compatible when they are equal or one has size one; missing leading axes act like ones. That convenience can silently create a pairwise operation: subtracting labels \([B]\) from predictions \([B, 1]\) (\(\text{predictions}-\text{labels}\)) produces \([B, B]\), rather than \(B\) individual residuals. Explicitly reshape labels, and assert named dimensions at module boundaries. Avoid a plain transpose on higher-dimensional tensors when only the feature and sequence axes should swap.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Pair the textbook's matrix notation with PyTorch's Broadcasting Semantics reference. For any proposed operation, write the semantic axis names above the shape before applying the documented compatibility rules. In the classifier example, \([16, 1]\) means sixteen examples with one prediction each, whereas \([16]\) means sixteen scalar labels. The accidental \([16, 16]\) result compares each prediction with every label, so the mistake is statistical as well as dimensional.

A useful independent check is to use two predictions, \(\begin{bmatrix}10\\20\end{bmatrix}\), and targets \([10, 20]\). The intended residuals are both zero, but broadcasting \(\text{predictions}-\text{targets}\) yields \(\begin{bmatrix}0&-10\\10&0\end{bmatrix}\). A successful operation has therefore implemented the wrong comparisons. Repeat the derivation after reshaping the targets to \([2, 1]\). This habit becomes especially valuable with attention masks, where a singleton placed on the wrong axis can produce a valid shape and an unintended information boundary.

exercise.prompt: A classifier produces \([16, 1]\) predictions and receives \([16]\) scalar targets. What shape does subtraction produce, and how should you fix it?
exercise.answer: Right-aligned broadcasting expands \([16]\) to \([1, 16]\), so the result is \([16, 16]\). Reshape targets to \([16, 1]\), or squeeze the final prediction dimension to \([16]\), before computing the elementwise loss.

takeaways: Name axes before deriving their sizes.
A valid broadcast can still implement the wrong objective.

title: Rank and singular values reveal what a layer can express
summary: Understand eigenvectors and the SVD through the directions a linear transformation preserves or removes.

sections.title: Look for informative directions
paragraphs: A matrix may have many entries but still produce outputs confined to a small subspace. Its rank counts independent output directions. If two rows encode the same measurement, adding both does not create a new degree of freedom. This matters when diagnosing redundant features, understanding compression, or asking why a low-rank weight update can be much smaller than a dense matrix while still changing useful model behavior.

sections.title: Separate rotation from scaling
paragraphs: An eigenvector of a square matrix is a nonzero vector mapped to a scalar multiple of itself. For real eigenvalues, a negative value reverses its direction and zero maps it to the zero vector. Some real matrices, such as a 90-degree planar rotation, have no real eigenvectors. The singular value decomposition works for rectangular matrices too: \(A=U\Sigma V^{\top}\). For the column-vector convention \(y=Ax\), a right singular vector \(v_i\) is mapped to \(\sigma_i u_i\): \(V\) specifies input directions and \(U\) output directions. In the row-vector convention \(y=xW\) used earlier, \(W=U\Sigma V^{\top}\) instead maps \(u_i^{\top}\) to \(\sigma_i v_i^{\top}\), so those roles swap. Keeping the largest \(r\) singular values gives the best rank-\(r\) approximation in Frobenius norm, although that matrix error does not directly guarantee task accuracy.

sections.title: Exact rank is not effective rank
paragraphs: For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&0.001\end{bmatrix}\), exact rank is two, but one direction is amplified two thousand times more than the other. Finite precision and noise may make the weak direction unusable. Numerical rank therefore depends on a tolerance and scale. Eigenvalues can also mislead for nonsymmetric matrices: singular values, rather than eigenvalue magnitudes alone, describe one-step worst-case amplification. Inspect the singular spectrum instead of reporting only a single integer.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the textbook's eigendecomposition and SVD discussions side by side, keeping square-matrix eigenvectors separate from singular vectors. For an additional check, consider \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&10\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). Its eigenvalues are both 1, yet multiplying \([0,1]^{\top}\) produces \([10,1]^{\top}\). The length grows to \(\sqrt{101}\). Eigenvalue magnitudes alone therefore miss the largest one-step amplification of this nonsymmetric map.

Use the singular-value example in this article to distinguish an approximation guarantee from an application guarantee. Discarding the singular value 2 gives a Frobenius error of 2, but a downstream task might rely entirely on that discarded direction. Conversely, a large discarded direction might mainly encode nuisance variation. When reading a compression paper, identify the matrix being approximated, the norm used to measure its error, and the separate experiment that measures task performance. A mathematical approximation bound and an accuracy result answer different questions.

exercise.prompt: A matrix has singular values \([5, 2, 0]\). What is its rank, and what Frobenius error results from retaining only the largest singular value?
exercise.answer: The rank is two. Removing singular values 2 and 0 leaves Frobenius error \(\sqrt{2^2+0^2}=2\). The squared error is 4; confusing error with squared error changes the reported quantity.

takeaways: Rank counts independent directions.
Singular values describe amplification and approximation error.

title: The chain rule is the wiring diagram of learning
summary: Connect partial derivatives, Jacobians, and backpropagation by tracking how small changes propagate.

sections.title: A derivative answers a local question
paragraphs: A partial derivative asks how an output changes when one input coordinate moves and the others stay fixed. A gradient collects those sensitivities for a scalar output. A Jacobian extends the idea to a vector output: each row describes one output coordinate and each column one input coordinate. These are local descriptions, so a derivative at today's parameters does not promise the same behavior after a large update.

sections.title: Compose sensitivities in the right order
paragraphs: Consider \(x\) mapped to \(z=Wx+b\), then \(h=\tanh(z)\), then a scalar loss. The derivative of the loss with respect to \(z\) multiplies the incoming gradient elementwise by \(1-\tanh^2(z)\). The derivative with respect to \(x\) is \(W^{\top}\) times that result. Backpropagation computes these vector-Jacobian products without constructing an enormous Jacobian explicitly. A shared variable receives a sum of contributions from every path that uses it.

sections.title: Check a derivative numerically
paragraphs: For \(f(w)=(3w-1)^2\), the derivative is \(6(3w-1)\). At \(w = 1\) it equals 12. Compare this with the centered difference \(\frac{f(w+\varepsilon)-f(w-\varepsilon)}{2\varepsilon}\). A moderate \(\varepsilon\) balances approximation error against floating-point cancellation. Use float64 for a small gradient check, avoid nondifferentiable points such as a ReLU kink, and check a few coordinates rather than assuming a successful backward call proves correctness.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Use Numerical Computation for derivative and Jacobian notation, then Deep Feedforward Networks for computational graphs and backpropagation. Translate each operation into a small dependency diagram before differentiating. For \(y=ab+a^2\), draw two routes from \(a\) to \(y\) and one from \(b\). This diagram explains the sum \(b + 2a\) without relying on a remembered formula, and the same reasoning applies when a shared embedding or projection is reused at many positions.

To connect that notation with numerical evidence, evaluate the centered difference at several step sizes rather than selecting one successful value. A large step can measure curvature beyond the local neighborhood, while an extremely small step can subtract nearly equal floating-point numbers. Agreement across a reasonable range is stronger evidence. Also inspect the point being tested: a ReLU at zero has no ordinary derivative, so a mismatch there does not necessarily reveal an implementation error.

exercise.prompt: Let \(y=ab+a^2\). Find both partial derivatives at \(a = 2\) and \(b = 3\). Why does the derivative with respect to \(a\) have two terms?
exercise.answer: \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial a}=b+2a=7\) and \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial b}=a=2\). The variable \(a\) affects \(y\) through both the product \(ab\) and the square \(a^2\), so the chain rule adds both path contributions.

takeaways: Gradients are local sensitivities.
Backpropagation accumulates contributions along every computational path.

title: Why a gradient step can lower the loss
summary: Derive the local descent argument and see why learning rate matters even for a simple quadratic.

sections.title: Follow a locally useful direction
paragraphs: The gradient points toward the steepest local increase under Euclidean distance. Moving in its negative direction therefore promises a decrease for a sufficiently small step when the gradient is nonzero. The word local is essential: the terrain can curve sharply, and a direction that looked helpful at the starting point may overshoot the useful region. Optimization repeatedly remeasures that direction instead of trusting one gradient forever.

sections.title: Use the first-order approximation
paragraphs:
For parameters \(	heta\) and a small displacement \(\Delta\), the loss is approximately \(L(	heta)+

abla LVert^2\). For \(L(w)= rac{aw^2}{2}\) with \(a > 0\), the update is exactly \(w_{	ext{next}}=(1-\eta a)w\). It converges when \(0<\eta a<2\). Larger curvature therefore requires a smaller stable step.

sections.title: Separate poor conditioning from noise
paragraphs: A loss bowl can be steep along one coordinate and shallow along another. One global learning rate then oscillates across the steep direction while making slow progress in the shallow direction. Feature scaling, adaptive optimizers, and momentum can change this behavior. Minibatch gradients add sampling noise, so a single increase in training loss is not proof of failure. Inspect smoothed trends, gradient norms, and validation performance before increasing the model's complexity.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Use the textbook's discussion of gradient descent to separate the proposed direction from the chosen distance. The local linear approximation predicts improvement along a negative gradient, but it does not choose a universally safe learning rate. The quadratic in this article makes that distinction exact: its multiplicative update factor is \(1-10\eta\). Convergence requires the magnitude of that factor to be less than one.

An instructive extension is a two-coordinate loss with very different curvatures, such as \(\frac{w_1^2+100w_2^2}{2}\). A learning rate suitable for the first coordinate may destabilize the second. Draw the two scalar update factors before attributing slow learning to an insufficiently expressive model. When comparing an optimizer paper with your own run, record feature scaling and loss reduction too: either can change effective curvature and make a quoted learning rate inappropriate.

exercise.prompt: For \(L(w)=5w^2\) and \(w = 1\), compare one gradient step with learning rates 0.1 and 0.3. Which step reduces the loss?
exercise.answer: The gradient is \(10w\). With \(\eta=0.1\), \(w\) becomes 0 and loss becomes 0. With \(\eta=0.3\), \(w\) becomes \(-2\) and loss rises from 5 to 20. The stable interval is \(0<\eta<0.2\).

takeaways: Negative gradients offer local descent, not a global guarantee.
Curvature and learning rate jointly determine stability.

title: Probability turns incomplete information into explicit assumptions
summary: Use conditional probability, Bayes' rule, expectation, and variance to reason about uncertain observations.

sections.title: Conditioning changes the question
paragraphs: A probability describes uncertainty under a specified information set. \(P(A)\) asks about an event before seeing evidence; \(P(A\mid B)\) asks after learning \(B\). These need not be similar. In machine learning, the training distribution supplies one information environment, while deployment may supply another. Writing the conditioning variables explicitly prevents ambiguous claims such as a model being accurate without saying on which examples or under which sampling process.

sections.title: Reverse a conditional with base rates
paragraphs: Suppose 10% of documents are technical. A keyword appears in 80% of technical documents and 20% of other documents. Among 100 imagined documents, 8 technical and 18 nontechnical documents contain it. The probability that a keyword-containing document is technical is therefore \(\frac8{26}\), about 0.308. It is not 0.8: that number answers the opposite conditional. Bayes' rule combines likelihood with the prior frequency of the event.

sections.title: Summarize a distribution carefully
paragraphs: Expectation is a probability-weighted average, not necessarily a possible observation. A Bernoulli outcome can only be zero or one, even when its expectation is 0.3. Variance measures expected squared deviation from the mean and has squared units. For sums, variances add only when covariance terms vanish; dependent training examples can therefore make uncertainty larger than an independent-sample calculation suggests. Always identify the random variable before taking its mean or variance.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the probability chapter with a distinction between a joint event and a conditional event. Reconstruct the keyword example as four cells: technical with keyword, technical without it, nontechnical with keyword, and nontechnical without it. Their probabilities are 0.08, 0.02, 0.18, and 0.72. Conditioning on the keyword keeps only the first and third cells and renormalizes their total.

Now change only the technical-document base rate to 0.5 while keeping the two keyword likelihoods fixed. The posterior becomes 0.8 rather than approximately 0.308. This is a useful interpretation exercise for any reported classifier performance: the frequency of relevant cases can change what a positive signal means. For the variance example, keep the units visible. Multiplying a measurement by four multiplies deviations by four and squared deviations by sixteen; it does not create sixteen independent observations.

exercise.prompt: A binary variable \(X\) equals 1 with probability 0.25. Compute \(\mathbb{E}[X]\), \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\). What changes for \(Y = 4X\)?
exercise.answer: \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]=0.25\), so \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.25-0.0625=0.1875\). For \(Y\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y]=1\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=16\cdot0.1875=3\). Scaling changes variance quadratically.

takeaways: Conditional probabilities depend on the direction of the question.
Expectation and variance describe different aspects of uncertainty.

title: Choose a distribution that matches the outcome
summary: Distinguish Bernoulli, categorical, and Gaussian models by their support and parameters.

sections.title: Start with what can happen
paragraphs: A distribution's support is the set of outcomes it can describe. A Bernoulli variable represents one binary outcome, a categorical variable selects one of several mutually exclusive classes, and a Gaussian variable represents a continuous measurement. Choosing a likelihood is therefore a modeling decision about the data. A classification head and a regression head differ partly because they assign probability to different kinds of outcomes.

sections.title: Connect outputs to valid parameters
paragraphs: A Bernoulli model needs a probability \(p\) between zero and one, often obtained with a sigmoid. A categorical model needs nonnegative probabilities that sum to one, usually produced by softmax logits. A Gaussian model needs a mean and a positive variance; predicting an unconstrained log-variance is one way to enforce positivity. Multiple independent binary labels generally require several Bernoulli outputs, not one categorical distribution that forces only one label to be correct.

sections.title: Probability density is not probability mass
paragraphs: A continuous variable assigns zero probability to any exact point. Its density can exceed one, while probabilities over intervals remain bounded by one. Consequently, comparing a Gaussian density value with a categorical class probability is meaningless. Gaussian residual assumptions also have limits: strong skew, heavy tails, or multiple modes can make a single mean-and-variance model misleading. Examine residuals and predicted uncertainty rather than assuming every continuous target is naturally Gaussian.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Use the probability chapter's distribution definitions to enumerate outcomes before selecting a model head. Two object-presence labels have four joint possibilities: neither object, either object alone, and both objects. Two sigmoid outputs can estimate the two marginal probabilities. Treating their product as a joint likelihood adds a conditional-independence modeling assumption; it does not establish that the objects are independent in real scenes.

For a continuous example, imagine a Gaussian concentrated tightly around zero. Its density near zero can exceed one because a density is converted into probability by integration over an interval. Changing measurement units also changes density values. These observations explain why a raw regression density should not be compared with a classification probability as if both were confidence percentages. When a paper reports a likelihood, identify the outcome space, units, distribution family, and any factorization assumptions before interpreting its numerical scale.

exercise.prompt: An image can contain both a dog and a bicycle. Should two output scores use a two-class softmax or independent sigmoids? Explain the outcome space.
exercise.answer: Use independent sigmoids for the two presence labels, allowing neither, either, or both objects. A two-class softmax allows only one class and forces the probabilities to sum to one, excluding valid joint outcomes.

takeaways: Match distribution support to the prediction task.
A density and a probability mass are different quantities.

title: Maximum likelihood chooses parameters that explain observed data
summary: Derive familiar losses by writing down a probabilistic model and maximizing its likelihood.

sections.title: Fit a model to the observations
paragraphs: Maximum likelihood estimates parameters by asking which setting assigns the greatest probability, or density, to the observed dataset. The data are fixed during this optimization; the parameters vary. This differs from treating the likelihood as a probability distribution over parameters. To make a likelihood meaningful, specify the outcome distribution and assumptions about dependence between examples before choosing an optimizer.

sections.title: Products become sums of log probabilities
paragraphs: For independent Bernoulli observations, the likelihood multiplies \(p\) for every success and \(1-p\) for every failure. Taking logs turns the product into a sum, which is easier to optimize and less vulnerable to numerical underflow. Differentiating that sum shows that the maximum-likelihood estimate is the empirical success rate. For a Gaussian with fixed variance, maximizing log likelihood is equivalent to minimizing squared residuals; changing the distribution changes the loss.

sections.title: Likelihood does not protect against overfitting
paragraphs: A flexible model can assign high likelihood to training examples by memorizing peculiarities that do not recur. Evaluate on held-out data and consider regularization or a prior when data are limited. With all Bernoulli observations equal to one, MLE gives \(p = 1\), assigning zero probability to any future failure. That boundary estimate illustrates why finite data can produce overconfident conclusions even when the optimization is mathematically correct.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Locate the maximum-likelihood construction in Machine Learning Basics, then derive the Bernoulli example without treating likelihood as a distribution over \(p\). Seven successes and three failures give a parameter-dependent term \(p^7(1-p)^3\). Taking its logarithm produces \(7\log p+3\log(1-p)\); the stationary point is \(p = 0.7\). This connects the probability model directly to the scalar objective an optimizer receives.

A useful boundary case is a dataset containing only successes. The optimum occurs at \(p = 1\), not at an interior point where the same stationary-point argument applies. The data do not guarantee that failure is impossible, even though the fitted model assigns it zero probability. For regression, check whether variance is fixed before claiming that Gaussian likelihood is equivalent to squared-error minimization. Learning the variance introduces additional terms and a different optimization problem.

exercise.prompt: You observe 7 successes and 3 failures. What is the Bernoulli MLE? If the next observation is a failure, what is its negative log likelihood under that estimate?
exercise.answer: The estimate is \(p=\frac7{10}=0.7\). A failure has probability 0.3, so its negative log likelihood is \(-\ln(0.3)\), approximately 1.204 nats. The logarithm base determines the unit.

takeaways: A loss function often encodes a likelihood assumption.
Maximum training likelihood does not guarantee generalization.

title: Entropy, cross-entropy, and KL answer three different questions
summary: Separate intrinsic uncertainty from the penalty for using the wrong predictive distribution.

sections.title: Measure surprise under a distribution
paragraphs: An event with low predicted probability has high surprise, measured as negative log probability. Entropy averages that surprise when the predictions equal the true distribution \(p\). Cross-entropy averages surprise when outcomes still come from \(p\) but a different distribution \(q\) supplies the predictions. KL divergence isolates the extra expected surprise caused by that mismatch. This distinction explains why a nonzero optimal loss need not mean a model is wrong.

sections.title: Decompose the prediction cost
paragraphs: Expanding the definitions gives \(H(p,q)=H(p)+\operatorname{KL}(p\Vert q)\). When \(p\) is fixed, minimizing cross-entropy also minimizes this forward KL because entropy does not depend on model parameters. For a fair binary source, a correct predictor still has entropy \(\ln2\). A predictor \(q = [0.9, 0.1]\) incurs higher cross-entropy because it confidently favors one outcome without evidence. KL is directional, so reversing \(p\) and \(q\) changes the weighting of errors.
sections.formula: H(p)=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i;\qquad H(p,q)=-\sum_i p_i\log q_i

sections.title: One-hot labels simplify, but do not redefine, the objective
paragraphs: With a one-hot observed label, cross-entropy reduces to \(-\log q(\text{correct})\). Averaging over examples estimates an expectation over the underlying data distribution; it does not prove that the true conditional entropy is zero. Never apply softmax twice when a loss expects logits, and distinguish mean from summed loss when comparing runs. If \(q\) assigns zero probability where \(p\) is positive, the forward KL is infinite rather than merely large.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Use the information-theory definitions in the probability chapter to keep the distribution generating outcomes separate from the distribution scoring them. Write one table with columns for \(p\), \(q\), \(-\log p\), and \(-\log q\). Weight both surprise columns by \(p\). This makes the entropy/cross-entropy distinction visible and prevents accidentally reversing the KL direction when translating between a paper's notation and a training loss.

For a concrete extension, retain \(p = [0.5, 0.5]\) but use \(q = [0.9, 0.1]\). Cross-entropy is approximately 1.204 nats and the excess over \(\ln2\) is approximately 0.511 nats. Those values describe expected predictive surprise, not classification accuracy: a deterministic choice from \(q\) can hide the probability calibration problem. When comparing losses, also check logarithm base, averaging denominator, and whether the targets are empirical one-hot observations or an explicitly supplied soft distribution.

exercise.prompt: For \(p = [0.5, 0.5]\) and \(q = [0.5, 0.5]\), calculate entropy, cross-entropy, and KL using natural logs. What does their relationship tell you?
exercise.answer: Entropy and cross-entropy both equal \(\ln2\approx0.693\) nats, while KL is zero. Prediction is distributionally correct despite positive loss, because the source itself remains uncertain.

takeaways: Cross-entropy equals entropy plus forward KL.
Zero KL can coexist with positive predictive loss.

title: Optimizers differ in how they turn gradients into steps
summary: Understand SGD, momentum, Adam, and AdamW through the state each optimizer carries.

sections.title: A gradient is only the starting signal
paragraphs: SGD scales the current minibatch gradient by a learning rate. Momentum adds a running directional memory, smoothing noisy updates and allowing progress along consistently useful directions. Adam maintains both a first moment and a second moment of gradients, adapting the step scale per coordinate. These choices change the optimization trajectory, even when models, batches, and losses are identical.

sections.title: Track moments and decay separately
paragraphs: Adam's first moment averages gradients; its second moment averages squared gradients. Bias correction compensates for both moving averages starting at zero. The normalized update divides the corrected first moment by the square root of the corrected second moment plus a stabilizing epsilon. AdamW additionally shrinks weights independently of that adaptive normalization. An \(L_2\) penalty added to the gradient is equivalent to weight decay in simple SGD under matching conventions, but generally not in Adam.

sections.title: Compare complete training configurations
paragraphs: A comparison between optimizers is incomplete without learning rate, schedule, batch size, decay, and training budget. Adam's extra moment tensors also consume memory; changing only the optimizer may alter the largest feasible batch. Watch update norms as well as gradient norms, because adaptive scaling can produce very different parameter changes from similar gradients. When resuming training, restore optimizer state or acknowledge that the next steps no longer continue the original trajectory.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the Adam update algorithm before its reported benchmark results. Follow one coordinate through the first update: starting both moments at zero and applying bias correction makes the corrected first moment equal \(g\) and the corrected second moment equal \(g^2\). The resulting step is approximately a signed learning-rate-sized move when \(\lvert g\rvert\) is much larger than epsilon. This helps explain why raw gradient magnitude does not directly determine an Adam update.

Compare AdamW's regularization with an explicit implementation. Does shrinkage enter the gradient before moment estimation, or change the parameter separately? These alternatives leave different optimizer histories, so matching a nominal decay coefficient does not make them equivalent. Preserve parameter-group settings and restore moments and step counts when resuming.

Finally, read Reddi, Kale, and Kumar's analysis alongside Adam's original convergence claim. They identify a flaw in that proof and construct convex counterexamples to convergence. This limits the original guarantee; it does not imply that Adam fails on every practical task.

exercise.prompt: Why does loading only model weights fail to resume an Adam training run exactly? Name two missing pieces of optimizer state.
exercise.answer: Adam's running first and second moments are missing, along with its step count for bias correction. Reinitializing them changes the normalized updates even if the next batch, weights, and learning rate are identical.

takeaways: Optimizer state affects both trajectory and memory.
AdamW separates weight shrinkage from adaptive gradient scaling.

title: Generalization begins with how you split the data
summary: Use training, validation, and test sets to separate fitting, model selection, and final measurement.

sections.title: Training success is an incomplete result
paragraphs: A model is useful when it performs on examples it did not fit. Overfitting means fitting training-specific patterns that fail to generalize to fresh examples from the same data-generating distribution. A deployment failure can also arise from distribution shift, and leakage can make an evaluation misleading; neither is by itself evidence of overfitting. More training accuracy is therefore evidence about fitting capacity, not sufficient evidence that a model is ready for a new population.

sections.title: Give each split one job
paragraphs: Training data determine parameter updates. Validation data guide choices such as hyperparameters, architecture, and stopping time. Test data estimate performance after those choices are fixed. The split unit must match the independence assumption: if several scans belong to one patient, randomizing scans can place near-related examples on both sides. For forecasting, chronological separation is often more meaningful than random splitting because future information would not be available at prediction time.

sections.title: Regularization changes the effective search
paragraphs: Weight decay, dropout, augmentation, early stopping, and architectural constraints restrict or reshape the functions training tends to produce. None repairs a leaked test set. Fit preprocessing statistics on training data only, keep duplicates and related groups together, and record every validation-driven choice. Repeatedly checking the test set and selecting the best run turns that set into another validation set. Report variation across sensible seeds when training randomness materially affects conclusions.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Use Machine Learning Basics to separate the learning algorithm's training sample from the population on which generalization is measured. In the person-level example, ten measurements from one individual are not ten independent tests of performance on unseen people. Assigning a person to a split before selecting their measurements preserves the intended evaluation question. A measurement-level random split answers a different, usually easier question.

When reading a result table, reconstruct the decisions made with validation data: architecture selection, preprocessing, stopping time, and checkpoint choice can all adapt the system to that split. The test set estimates performance only after those choices are fixed. If a deployment population differs substantially, a clean held-out test from the original population may still be insufficient. Distinguish that distribution shift from overfitting so the proposed remedy addresses the observed failure rather than merely reducing model capacity.

exercise.prompt: A dataset contains 100 people with 10 measurements each. You want performance on unseen people. Why is a random measurement-level split misleading, and what split should replace it?
exercise.answer: Measurements from the same person can share identity-specific information, so the model may recognize people instead of generalizing. Split by person, placing all 10 measurements together, then fit preprocessing only on the training group.

takeaways: Choose a split unit that matches deployment.
Regularization cannot compensate for evaluation leakage.
